Hello, relatively new to Lean here.

What options are there for manipulating the DOM from Lean? I imagine I would need a model of the DOM, then an Elm-like model-view-update loop, then a way to call JavaScript to do this manipulation.

What's the state of the art? Who's working on this?

I think it might be possible to compile Lean to WASM, but I'm not sure.

I found several projects that roughly do this, but they all look very early stages.
https://github.com/theoriclabs/lean-react
https://github.com/ejgallego/lean-vir
https://github.com/JacobAsmuth/qed

A concrete place to look at for the DOM model is ProofWidgets4. ProofWidgets.Html (ProofWidgets/Data/Html.lean) already has element, text and component (React components with JSON props), and there's JSX support too, so you can do open scoped ProofWidgets.Jsx and then <div>xyz</div>. Uppercase tags are components.

It's used in the VS Code infoview rather than as a standalone web page, but it's probably the most mature HTML type in Lean right now.

For WASM I can only speak from using hand-written WASM on a website, not from building Lean to WASM. In general the page needs 'wasm-unsafe-eval' in the CSP, and I'd use SRI and WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming for loading it. Size is also something to watch out for, since the Lean runtime is already a few mb.

The usual setup could be something like the WASM module exporting a pure update function and JS handling the view. We've also kept a WASM implementation in sync with a JS reference before, which caught quite a few bugs.

I haven't tried the Lean-to-WASM build myself though, so I don't know how rough that part is at the moment.

@West , lean-vir is for now FRO-internal, but it will very likely improved to a more suitable form for external users in Q4 2026.

lean-vir (and sister project lean-fir) does work by compiling a subset of Lean to WASM. You can manipulate DOM from there using regular WASM to JS bridges. We provide some tooling for this, and an experimental bindings surface where a type Js Bar means "an JS object of type Bar is living in the JS heap.

There is not formal model of the DOM in VIR or FIR. lean-fir does interact with the Talos WASM model and targets it.

I completely forgot about proofwidgets, so thank you for reminding me @JoelCanary.

I'll definitely try out lean-vir @Emilio Jesús Gallego Arias. Good to know it's actively being worked on.

@West note that DOM binding syntax and types is expected to change / evolve.

If you are interested in "pure" Lean programs running in WASM, the surface is much more stable.

In my tests, simple pure lean can already be used as a language for mathematical computation directly in the browser, but at the moment, running Lean through a WebAssembly interpreter comes with a huge performance cost
@JoelCanary have you been using lean-vir for your experiments? If yes, what kind of examples?

Emilio Jesús Gallego Arias dijo:

JoelCanary have you been using lean-vir for your experiments? If yes, what kind of examples?

Yes, it's a Lean-vir repo with 8 small math problems, benchmarked against native and JS: https://github.com/joelcanary/lean-math-in-the-browser

@JoelCanary, thank you very much for the benchmarks and independent verification. This is very helpful, and your results match my local measurements.

VIR's primary use case is to replace the small pieces of JavaScript often needed in Verso and widget authoring with Lean code. We chose the IR interpreter for simplicity and ease of maintenance: in most of these use cases, its overhead is small, a reasonable trade-off for a simpler toolchain and authoring workflow.

That said, I agree that VIR’s approach can only take us so far in terms of performance. That’s the motivation behind FIR, which generates WebAssembly directly. FIR is still very experimental, and it’s not yet clear whether it will be supported in the long term, but so far I’m very happy with it: it provides a non-interpreted execution path, which can make a meaningful difference.

A third approach is to use Emscripten, which @Fawad has used with great success in QED64. This path now supports the full Lean runtime. FIR’s tooling also supports it as a baseline for comparison, though it comes with important trade-offs.

I also asked Codex to rerun your benchmarks with FIR and FIR-C (our name for the Emscripten path). The results are here: https://github.com/ejgallego/lean-math-in-the-browser/blob/research/vir-fir-report/docs/REPORT.md

Your bench already identified a few slow paths in FIR (mostly on the bignums parts), Astra should get back to us with a much faster version in a while.

[Disclaimer, the results are AI generated, using my standard tooling, I did only review them lightly]

Let me know what you think, feedback is very important!

Thanks @Emilio Jesús Gallego Arias Glad QED64 is getting noticed. I didn't know about lean-vir, lean-fir going to wasm from lean IR is a very interesting approach. I used that for RISCV cross compilation but never thought of wasm. Will look into the FIR project more. I have a lot of widgets built (with AI help) that I wanted to showcase with the help QED64, just didn't know how much interest it would generate.

Would love to see benchmarks on QED64 as well. May be I will do a PR @JoelCanary

For anyone interested https://github.com/FawadHa1der/QED64, deployed at https://qed64.fawadworkaddress.workers.dev/ and the game version https://lean4game.fawadworkaddress.workers.dev/

Thanks Emilio! I think the review was really useful and fair. You found two real issues in my benchmark, and i fixed them here:

https://github.com/joelcanary/lean-math-in-the-browser/blob/main/docs/REPORT.md#corrections-28-september-2026

The good thing is that the corrections don't change the main results. The numbers are still in the same order of magnitude.

I also think VIR makes a lot of sense for Verso and widgets. For small inputs it is already quite fast, and the startup in Chrome was around 55 ms in our test. FIR looks very promising for bigger computations, especially loops and arrays. The bignum cases seem to be a weaker point for now.

I'd be happy to run the benchmarks again when the new FIR version is available. Also, feel free to use my 40 test inputs with the independent reference values.

One thing I'm curious about: how big is FIR in the browser, and what input sizes are typical for Verso?

@Fawad, yes, we've seen QED64, stunning work! Congratulations to you and everyone who contributed on such an impressive technical achievement.

The history of Lean and WASM is quite interesting. Emscripten was officially supported for a while, but the move to a more complex runtime with asynchronous parallelism made that support difficult to maintain. Meanwhile, mathlib's growing size became another obstacle to browser use.

With agentic coding, Lean’s module system, improvements in Emscripten, and projects like QED64, running Lean fully in the browser looks increasingly practical again. It's exciting to see!

VIR is an official FRO project, though it is still internal. The goal is to provide a simple, easy-to-maintain way to run Lean in the browser without any extra tooling. Lean’s IR interpreter is a C++ program that compiles cleanly to WASM with LLVM + WASI, and that compilation only needs to happen once per Lean toolchain.

We purposely ship a small IR runtime (< 200KiB), but with quite a good coverage power. See:

  • https://ejgallego.github.io/lean-vir/size
  • https://ejgallego.github.io/lean-vir/surface/

For more details about VIR's runtime size and Lean Stdlib coverage.

Unfortunately, VIR's performance fell short for some of our internal use cases. Illuminate is one example; lean-zip also illustrates the interpreter overhead well.

I had some spare tokens over the summer holidays, so I asked Codex to built a simple compiler, that became FIR (VIR = Virtual IR, FIR = Formal IR).

It's still entirely experimental, but so far it has worked really well for the performance issues I was running into. I hope to write more about it before the end of 2026. In brief, it's a proof-driven compiler from LCNF to WASM, with a custom runtime and, again, no external dependencies.

Would love to see benchmarks on QED64 as well. May be I will do a PR JoelCanary

Looking forward to see these numbers!

The updated benchmark results on my side include my simple Emscripten-based compilation path in the C/Wasm column. These measurements were taken in Node rather than in a browser, but should give an rough idea on where Lean -> C -> WASM via LLVM stands.

I think FIR is doing quite well for such a simple compiler, although there are still clear gaps. We generate WASM after Lean's full optimization pipeline, so we benefit from all the performance work already done there.

@JoelCanary, yes, those were minor issues and didn't affect the benchmark numbers. The updated results are linked above. There are still a few cases to optimize, and your benchmark data is really helpful in identifying them, thanks!

how big is FIR in the browser, and what input sizes are typical for Verso?

FIR currently builds monolithic packages, so the size depends on the package and its dependency closure. Typical sizes in my experiments range from 300KiB (lean-zip) to a few MiB (Verso React renderer). I haven't tried any size optimization there, so it should be possible to do better, and of course, compress.

For Verso, my largest test is rendering the FLT Blueprint Port to React—roughly 100 pages. In that test, FIR takes about 300 ms and VIR about 600 ms. The relative performance gap is surprisingly modest in this case, but I expect it to become more pronounced as we optimize the WASM-to-DOM path, which is currently slow, particularly when building props.

I should note that another path for Lean to WASM exists, using WASI instead of Emscripten, driven by @Shachar Itzhaky , and which has seen a lot of impressive effort too.

Let me know, folks, whether FIR or VIR could help with your use cases. Thanks again for the cool work and the benchmarks!

import Mathlib

namespace Showcase
open Finset Real Filter Topology

/-- Gauss: 0 + 1 + ⋯ + n = n(n+1)/2, by induction. -/
theorem gauss_sum (n : ℕ) : ∑ i ∈ range (n + 1), (i : ℚ) = n * (n + 1) / 2 := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp
  | succ n ih =>
    rw [sum_range_succ, ih]
    push_cast
    ring
Open in QED64 · runs Lean 4 + Mathlib in desktop Chrome or Firefox, nothing is uploaded

Yes it imports the full umbrella that was baked/snapshotted(that's half of mathlib currently). The required engineering for just downloading the few umbrellas is not worth it because Lean needs the whole dependency tree anyways. So one import could mean 1000 modules. Like import Mathlib.Tactic.Linarith requires 2 thousand modules(I could be wrong). A snapshot in QED parlance means everything serialized into wasm64 memory and preparing that snapshot requires 30-1 hour currently, so doing that for every different set of imports seems infeasible. I mean I can look at it further but that was my initial assessment. Feel free to push back etc
